fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title":"Falsifiable Or It Doesn't Count","body":"Chance Garton opens by admitting he once believed the Tartaria material, then sets a rule for the whole episode: a claim only counts if it can be checked and possibly disproven. He and Dylan Saccoccio read the Tartaria Britannica article on 999 Queen Street in full, break it into ten numbered assertions, and throw out the ones that are only mood, such as calling the asylum a fortress. The rest get tested against architects' journals, blueprints, tenders, newspapers and annual reports. Garton says he did everything short of flying to Ontario to dig through undigitized archives himself."},{"title":"Receipts From 999 Queen Street","body":"Against the claim of an oddly thin paper trail, Garton points to a cornerstone laid on August 22, 1846 by Chief Justice John Beverley Robinson, with engraved silver plaques recovered when the building came down in the 1970s. He shows blueprints digitized by the Toronto Public Library, a 2019 dissertation by Maximilian Smith quoting contractor John Ritchie's winning tender of 32,934 pounds against a final cost of 75,146 pounds, and Howard's journals held in the Baldwin Room. The wings came later, between 1866 and 1870, and the grand portico was never built at all."},{"title":"Why They Chose Provo","body":"Turning to JonLevi's video on the Utah State Hospital, Garton answers the question of why anyone would build there. Newspapers from 1880 and 1881 record counties bidding for the asylum, with Provo City offering 500 dollars and Utah County another 2,000, and a committee picking land watered by a mountain spring. The Utah Southern Railroad had reached Provo by 1873. Architect John H. Burton was 24 when appointed, toured asylums in Illinois, Indiana and Ohio in 1882, and was shot dead a day after turning 30. His apprentice Richard Kletting designed most of the building."},{"title":"Architecture Prescribed As Medicine","body":"Both hosts settle on a plain reason for the grandeur. Nineteenth century reformers followed the Kirkbride plan and its moral treatment, believing that light, clean air, symmetry and landscaping away from the city could actually cure insanity, which Garton likens to terrain theory. Toronto's dome was a water tower holding 12,000 gallons pumped from Lake Ontario, feeding hot and cold water through the wards by 1850, and patients built over 2,000 feet of the surrounding wall because labor was prescribed as therapy. A 1930s WPA remodel stripped Provo's spires to reduce the stigma of a castle."},{"title":"Grief Mistaken For Evidence","body":"Garton argues the genre runs on a reusable template, quoting a list from a member named Tonnie: flat disbelief, cherry picked photographs, the population was too small, there are no records, this old map proves something. He notes Levi calling New Deal buildings disguised old world architecture while the record dates the Provo amphitheater to a WPA project of 1936 and 1937, then retreating to saying he does not know. Saccoccio says that undermines you completely. Garton closes by insisting the debunk does not touch the feelings underneath, which he names as grief and anger."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Everyone in the Tartaria and mudflood space points at the giant 1800s insane asylums: too big, too grand, built too fast, records too thin. So I went and found the records. Full show notes linked at the bottom of the post (80 page document).
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: This is a full evidence check on two of the most talked-about asylum castles in North America: the Toronto Provincial Lunatic Asylum at 999 Queen Street West, tested against the claims of a popular Tartaria website, and the Utah Territorial Insane Asylum in Provo, tested against a 90,000-view JonLevi video. We go through the architects' journals, the original blueprints, the contractor's bid, the newspaper fights between counties, the cornerstone plaques recovered from the rubble, and the murdered architect that nobody in this genre ever bothered to look up. I used to believe this stuff. I wanted it to be true. What does paper trail actually show? A verdict on whether the old world civilization cover-up has any plausibility at all.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Receipts Nobody Wanted to Read", "body": "Once Levi is set aside, the show turns to the dullest evidence available and finds it decisive. The 1886 Biennial Report of the Board of Directors and Medical Superintendent of the Insane Asylum of Utah Territory names Warren Dusenbury as president, credits supervising architect John H. Burton, and itemises disbursements for excavation, plumbing, furniture and contract labour paid to a named carpenter and mason. Henry Hurd's multivolume survey of institutional care, compiled around 1916, then catalogues the same architecture across the continent, which makes the Provo building ordinary rather than anomalous. Ledgers are boring, and that is exactly why they are so hard to fake."}, {"title": "A Codified Plan, Not a Vanished Civilization", "body": "Carla Yanni's book hands the conversation the vocabulary it had been missing. Thomas Story Kirkbride, a Philadelphia Quaker physician, and the Association of Medical Superintendents of American Institutions for the Insane, founded in 1844, published numbered architectural propositions in 1851 and spread them through an illustrated how to book. At least thirty similar asylums followed before 1866 and roughly seventy by 1890. The spooky sameness of these castles turns out to be a franchise, executed by a small circle of doctors and architects who corresponded with each other and recommended each other for the next commission in the next state."}, {"title": "Environmental Determinism Was Terrain Medicine", "body": "The reform ideology behind all that grandeur has a name, and it turns out to be terrain theory wearing a different coat. Nineteenth century physicians believed light, air, symmetry and landscaping were part of the cure rather than decoration, so wards were built deliberately larger than the patient count, married attendant couples were housed on site, and patients moved toward the center of the building as they improved. The next century knocked the towers off, swapped the philosophy for medication, and replaced the cathedrals with drywall and parking lots. The suppression story here is medical, not Tartarian."}, {"title": "Doctor Bemis and the Fight the Record Preserves", "body": "If a national building programme really happened, there should be arguments about it somewhere, and there are. Merrick Bemis ran Worcester State Hospital from 1856 to 1872, had once been Kirkbride's own patient, visited Gheel in Belgium where families boarded the mentally ill, and came home convinced the linear plan was wrong at its core. His cottage proposal inverted the hierarchy by moving recovering patients outward instead of inward. Isaac Ray and Pliny Earle pushed back in writing, disputes over his finances piled up, he resigned in 1872, and the trustees quietly built a Kirkbride anyway."}, {"title": "Old Main Is Still Standing in Utica", "body": "The New York State Lunatic Asylum was designed by William Clark, a local entrepreneur, army captain and lottery operator whose quadrangle plan proved far too ambitious to finish. Patients printed a literary journal called The Opal from 1851 to 1860 and sold it to outside subscribers, the asylum ran an annual fair from 1844, President Millard Fillmore visited in 1851, and the entire state legislature toured the place. An arsonist named Spears, a former patient turned employee, set the 1857 fire that killed a doctor and a firefighter. The building survives today as a records archive."}]
